title.rendered: Food Prices in Mogadishu: Fish vs. Camel Meat

content.rendered:
In Mogadishu, a kilo of camel meat costs $5.50, while a kilo of fish costs $3.00. Camel meat costs $2.50 more per kg, or about 83% more than fish.

Key figures

  • Fish: $3.00 per kg
  • Camel meat: $5.50 per kg
  • Difference: $2.50 per kg

Why it matters

Somalia has one of the longest coastlines in Africa, yet fish is still a small part of most diets. At almost half the price of camel meat, fish is a cheaper source of protein for families facing rising food costs.

Source: SRA market check, Mogadishu, November 2026.

title.rendered: Somalia’s Cost of Living: What Got More Expensive in 2026?

content.rendered:
Prices for education, healthcare, housing and food were all higher in September 2026 than a year earlier. Education costs rose the fastest, by 11.5%, about twice as fast as food prices.

Key figures (annual price increase, September 2026)

  • Education: 11.5%
  • Healthcare: 9.6%
  • Housing: 9.2%
  • Food: 5.6%

Why it matters

Education, healthcare, housing and food take up most of a household’s budget. When school fees and health costs rise faster than incomes, families have to cut back on other needs.

Source: Somalia National Bureau of Statistics (SNBS), Consumer Price Index, September 2026; compiled by the Somali Researchers Association (SRA).

title.rendered: Baseline and endline surveys for a WASH project in Kismayo

content.rendered:
The Somali Researchers Association (SRA) conducted the baseline and endline surveys for INTERSOM’s WASH project in Kismayo, Lower Juba, funded by the Somalia Humanitarian Fund (SHF). The project provided water, sanitation and hygiene services to displaced families and host communities affected by climate shocks.

ClientINTERSOM
FundingSomalia Humanitarian Fund (SHF)
LocationKismayo district, Lower Juba
SRA’s roleBaseline and endline surveys

Two surveys, one project

SRA measured conditions at the start of the project and again at the end, in Nasrudin and Kanjiroon IDP camps and in the host communities of Turqato and Tulo Barwaqo. Comparing the two showed what the project changed for families.

BASELINE

Before the project

25 July – 10 August 2024

  • Household survey across the four locations
  • 8 focus group discussions, held separately with women and men
  • 12 key informant interviews with IDP, women and community leaders
  • 25 enumerators trained, 13 women and 12 men
ENDLINE

After the project

5 – 30 September 2025

  • Household survey across the same four locations
  • Focus group discussions and key informant interviews
  • Direct observation of water points, latrines and hygiene practices
  • Results compared with the baseline to measure change

What SRA delivered

For both surveys, SRA designed the tools, trained the enumerators, collected the data in the field, analysed it and wrote the reports. The endline assessed the project’s relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, sustainability and impact across water supply, sanitation and hygiene promotion.

content.rendered:

title.rendered: Somalia: Government Administration Spending (2025)

content.rendered:
In 2025, the Ministry of Finance alone spent $93.1 million in the administration and general services sector. The other 34 government institutions in the same sector spent $130.3 million combined. One ministry’s spending equals 71.5% of all 34 others together.

Key figures

  • Ministry of Finance: $93.1 million

The figures cover the administration and general services sector only. When a single ministry accounts for such a large share of administrative spending, it raises questions about how resources are divided across government, and how much reaches the other 34 institutions that deliver public services.

title.rendered: Somalia: Government Domestic Revenue, Budget Target vs Actual Collection (2023–2025)

content.rendered:
Somalia’s federal government collected more domestic revenue than it planned in 2023 and 2024. In 2025 the trend reversed: it collected $404.3 million against a budget target of $430.3 million, falling $26.0 million (6.0%) short.

Key figures

  • 2023: target $283.3 million, collected $329.5 million, which is $46.2 million (16.3%) above target
  • 2024: target $346.2 million, collected $369.4 million, which is $23.2 million (6.7%) above target
  • 2025: target $430.3 million, collected $404.3 million, which is $26.0 million (6.0%) below target

Why it matters

Revenue still grew every year, from $329.5 million in 2023 to $404.3 million in 2025. But the 2025 target was raised by about 24% over 2024, while actual collection grew by about 9%. A shortfall means less money than planned for salaries, services and development, and more reliance on donor support.

Sources: Somali Revenue Directorate, Ministry of Finance and IMF; compiled by the Somali Researchers Association (SRA).

Published by the Somali Researchers Association (SRA). See all our flash cards.

excerpt.rendered: Somalia’s domestic revenue beat the budget target in 2023 and 2024, but in 2025 the government collected $404.3 million against a target of $430.3 million: $26.0 million (6.0%) short.

title.rendered: Opening doors for young researchers: SRA and the Ministry of Planning

content.rendered:
SRA sits between two networks. On one side are Somali researchers, senior and junior. On the other are the institutions that need research: government ministries, UN agencies and businesses. SRA’s job is to connect them. When the Ministry of Planning wanted young researchers, it came to SRA.

Researchers

  • Senior and junior researchers
  • Guests of the Cilmi iyo Cod podcast
  • Authors in our journal, HAJOS
  • Enumerators across Somalia
⇄
SRAConnects, matches and supports research for all stakeholders
⇄

Institutions

  • Federal and state ministries
  • UN agencies and NGOs
  • Banks, telecoms and other businesses
  • Universities and hospitals

The opportunity

The Monitoring and Evaluation Department of the Ministry of Planning, Investment and Economic Development launched a platform to bring young researchers closer to government. Its aim: give early-career researchers a chance to present policy-relevant evidence to decision makers, receive feedback, and compete for small research grants for two of them, who would also present at the Ministry’s M&E conference.

The Ministry knew that SRA keeps a pool of senior and junior researchers, so it asked SRA to put junior researchers forward.

How SRA delivered

Request. The Ministry’s M&E Department asked SRA for junior researchers.

Match. SRA selected researchers from its pool, most of them Cilmi iyo Cod guests, whose work fitted the Ministry’s priorities.

Submit. Six junior researchers, four men and two women, from several universities, entered the competition.

Present. Four were shortlisted, including both women, to present to officials, academics and partners.

The result

Every researcher in the competition came from SRA’s network, so the two research grants will go to SRA researchers. Both the Ministry and the researchers thanked SRA for its work.

Why it matters

For young researchers

A direct route to decision makers: their evidence is heard by government, they get feedback, and they gain visibility and support for their next study.

For government and partners

A quick, trusted way to find capable researchers with ready evidence on national priorities, from health to governance.

Need researchers, a study or an evaluation? SRA connects ministries, UN agencies and businesses with the right researchers.

title.rendered: From SRA research to a UK courtroom

title.rendered: Somalia: Population Growth vs Real GDP Growth (2025)

content.rendered:
In 2025, Somalia’s population grew faster than its economy. The population grew by 3.34%, while real GDP grew by 3.1%, according to the World Bank and the Somalia National Bureau of Statistics (SNBS).

Key figures

  • Population growth: 3.34% (2025)
  • Real GDP growth: 3.1% (2025)
  • Gap: population growth is 0.24 percentage points higher than economic growth

Why it matters

When the population grows faster than the economy, the average income per person does not rise. With these figures, real GDP per person fell slightly, by about 0.2% in 2025. For living standards to improve, economic growth needs to stay above population growth.

Source: World Bank and Somalia National Bureau of Statistics (SNBS), 2025.

title.rendered: From SRA Data to Parliament: Hon. Faaisa Jeyte Raises the Ministry Salary Gap

content.rendered:
On 28 October 2026, Hon. Faaisa Jeyte, Member of the Federal Parliament, raised in Parliament the gap between what the Ministry of Finance pays its staff and what the three production ministries pay, and said it is not fair. The issue was highlighted in an SRA flash card based on the Federal Government’s own 2025 accounts.

What SRA found

In 2025 the Ministry of Finance spent $4.11 million on staff salaries, about 1.8 times the $2.29 million spent by the Ministries of Agriculture, Livestock and Fisheries combined.

  • Ministry of Finance: $4,113,110
  • Ministry of Agriculture and Irrigation: $900,450
  • Ministry of Fisheries and Blue Economy: $751,625
  • Ministry of Livestock, Forestry and Range: $641,290
  • The three production ministries combined: $2,293,365

Source: FGS 2025 Annual Financial Statements, Appendix 2. Wages and salaries only, excluding allowances and project spending.

Why it matters

Agriculture, livestock and fisheries are the sectors most Somalis earn their living from, yet the ministries that serve them spend far less on staff than the Ministry of Finance alone. SRA publishes short, sourced flash cards so that facts like this can reach the public and decision-makers. Seeing one raised in Parliament shows that independent evidence can shape the national debate.

title.rendered: Somalia’s Presidential Elections: Number of Candidates and Registration Fees (2012–2022)

content.rendered:
Somalia’s presidential elections have attracted more candidates over time, while the fee to register as a candidate has risen four times since 2012. Here are the numbers from the last three elections.

How many candidates ran for president?

  • 2012: 25 candidates
  • 2017: 24 candidates
  • 2022: 39 candidates

The 2022 field was 56% larger than in 2012, with 15 more candidates than in 2017.

How much does it cost to register as a candidate?

  • 2012: $10,000
  • 2017: $30,000
  • 2022: $40,000
  • 2027: not yet announced

The fee tripled between 2012 and 2017, then rose by another third in 2022. It is now four times higher than in 2012. For scale: if all 39 candidates in 2022 paid the $40,000 fee, registration fees would have totalled $1.56 million.

Key takeaways

  • More candidates are competing: 39 in 2022, the largest field so far.
  • Entering the race costs much more: $40,000 in 2022, up from $10,000 in 2012.
  • The 2027 fee will show whether this trend continues.

Source: Election documentation and media reports (2012, 2017, 2022).
